questions.stem: Where does energy first enter a food chain?

options.text: When producers turn light energy into chemical energy
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: When a top predator finally feeds
options.explanation: Top predators receive energy last; entry happens at producers.

options.text: When decomposers break down leaves
options.explanation: Decomposers recycle leftovers; entry happens at producers.

options.text: When rain washes minerals to roots
options.explanation: Minerals are substances, not the energy entry step.

questions.stem: In what form is light energy stored after producers capture it?

options.text: As electric charge in roots
options.explanation: Roots store no electric charge for the chain.

options.text: As chemical energy in carbon-containing compounds within their biomass
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: As heat inside the leaves
options.explanation: Heat is a loss pathway, not the storage form.

options.text: As sunlight trapped in chlorophyll
options.explanation: Chlorophyll captures light; storage lands in carbon compounds.

questions.stem: What does a primary consumer do with the carbon compounds in plant biomass?

options.text: It converts them back into light
options.explanation: Consumers never turn food back into light.

options.text: It releases them all as oxygen
options.explanation: Oxygen is not released from food this way.

options.text: It breaks them down and uses the energy and substances to build its own biomass
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: It stores them untouched forever
options.explanation: Digested compounds are rebuilt into consumer tissue, not shelved.

questions.stem: Which statement about substances along a food chain is correct?

options.text: Substances vanish completely at each level
options.explanation: Some are lost, but many transfer onward.

options.text: Substances travel only through water
options.explanation: Feeding, not water alone, moves them along the chain.

options.text: Substances stay locked in the producer
options.explanation: Feeding releases them to consumers.

options.text: Chemical substances are transferred between trophic levels as organisms feed
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: An owl eats a mouse that ate grass seeds. Trace the energy.

options.text: Light to grass, chemical energy into the mouse, then into the owl
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Owl gains light directly from the sun
options.explanation: Owls do not photosynthesise; energy arrives through prey.

options.text: Mouse gains energy from the owl
options.explanation: The arrow runs the other way.

options.text: Grass takes energy from the mouse
options.explanation: Grass is the source, not a receiver.

questions.stem: State the original energy source for every food chain.
questions.modelAnswer: The sun is the original source, with light energy converted to chemical energy by producers.

questions.stem: Name the compounds within producer biomass that store the captured energy.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon compounds held within the biomass of producers store the captured light energy.

questions.stem: Explain why the transfer of energy along a food chain is described as a flow.
questions.modelAnswer: The transfer is a flow because energy moves in one direction, from producers through each consumer level, and never returns to be reused by the level below.

questions.stem: A farmer grows cattle on pasture. Explain how solar energy reaches the beef.
questions.modelAnswer: Grass captures light energy into chemical energy in its biomass, and the cattle eat the grass and rebuild that energy into their own tissues.

questions.stem: Roughly what fraction of energy reaches the trophic level above?

options.text: 100 percent
options.explanation: Nothing transfers completely; losses always occur.

options.text: About 10 percent
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: About 50 percent
options.explanation: Half is far too generous; the figure is near a tenth.

options.text: About 90 percent
options.explanation: 90 percent is what is lost, not transferred.

questions.stem: Why does energy in bones and fur never reach the predator?

options.text: Because fur digests too quickly
options.explanation: Fur is not digested at all by most predators.

options.text: Because prey hide their bones
options.explanation: Hiding is not the mechanism; non-consumption is.

options.text: Because predators rarely eat every part of their prey, so uneaten parts keep their energy
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Because bones store no energy at all
options.explanation: Bones do store energy; it is simply never eaten.

questions.stem: Which route removes energy from a herbivore as heat?

options.text: Egestion of faeces
options.explanation: Faeces remove undigested material, not heat from respiration.

options.text: Growth of new muscle
options.explanation: Growth stores energy in biomass rather than losing it.

options.text: Photosynthesis in gut bacteria
options.explanation: Gut bacteria do not photosynthesise.

options.text: Respiration during movement and life processes
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: What happens to plant material a herbivore cannot digest?

options.text: It is egested as faeces, taking its energy out of the chain
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: It is fully absorbed into blood
options.explanation: Indigestible material is not absorbed.

options.text: It turns into muscle protein
options.explanation: Only digested material can build tissue.

options.text: It evaporates as water vapour
options.explanation: Faeces are solid waste, not vapour.

questions.stem: Why do food chains rarely exceed four or five levels?

options.text: Because consumers grow too heavy to move
options.explanation: Weight is irrelevant; energy scarcity ends the chain.

options.text: Because the remaining energy shrinks too far to support another trophic level
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Because predators refuse to eat each other
options.explanation: Predation continues; the energy limit decides.

options.text: Because producers run out of light at level four
options.explanation: Light reaches producers only, but the limit is energy shrinkage up the chain.

questions.stem: State the approximate percentage of energy transferred between trophic levels.
questions.modelAnswer: Only about 10 percent of the energy reaching one trophic level turns into biomass at the next.

questions.stem: Name the process that releases energy from food as heat inside consumers.
questions.modelAnswer: Respiration releases energy from digested food, much of it as heat, inside consumers.

questions.stem: Explain why excretion counts as an energy loss from a food chain.
questions.modelAnswer: Excretion counts as an energy loss because urea and other metabolic wastes carry energy that was absorbed but never converted into biomass.

questions.stem: A carnivore eats 1000 kJ of prey tissue and only 100 kJ builds its biomass. Give two reasons.
questions.modelAnswer: Roughly 900 kJ is lost because some prey parts were uneaten or undigested and egested, and respiration released much of the rest as heat.

questions.stem: Which two values divide in the efficiency equation?

options.text: Energy over time
options.explanation: Time is not part of the transfer equation.

options.text: Number of organisms over number of species
options.explanation: Counts and species belong to other measures.

options.text: Biomass in the higher trophic level over biomass in the lower trophic level
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Biomass in the lower level over the higher
options.explanation: That inverts the answer above 100 percent.

questions.stem: Clover holds 1450 kg of biomass and snails hold 138 kg. What is the transfer efficiency to three significant figures?

options.text: 95.2 percent
options.explanation: The decimal sits one place too high; 138 over 1450 times 100 is 9.52.

options.text: 105 percent
options.explanation: The higher level never exceeds the lower; check the division order.

options.text: 0.095 percent
options.explanation: The multiplication by 100 was skipped.

options.text: 9.52 percent
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: Why can energy efficiency reuse the biomass equation?

options.text: Because energy is stored within biomass, so the ratio behaves the same way
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Because energy and biomass are unrelated
options.explanation: They are closely related; energy sits inside biomass.

options.text: Because biomass is always measured in Joules
options.explanation: Biomass is measured in mass units, not Joules.

options.text: Because the exam board says so
options.explanation: The reason is physical, not administrative.

questions.stem: A level transfers 15 percent of its energy. What happens to the rest?

options.text: It returns to the sun
options.explanation: Energy radiates away as heat, not back to the sun.

options.text: It is lost to the environment through uneaten parts, egestion, heat and excretion
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: It is stored for the next year
options.explanation: No storage bank holds lost energy for later.

options.text: It becomes extra biomass
options.explanation: Only the transferred fraction builds biomass.

questions.stem: Thrushes hold 14.1 kg above snails at 138 kg. Which calculation gives their efficiency?

options.text: 14.1 times 138
options.explanation: Multiplication never yields a percentage.

options.text: 14.1 minus 138, times 100
options.explanation: Subtraction is not the efficiency formula.

options.text: 14.1 divided by 138, times 100, giving about 10.2 percent
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: 138 divided by 14.1, times 100
options.explanation: That inverts the ratio and exceeds 100 percent.

questions.stem: State the equation for the efficiency of biomass transfer.
questions.modelAnswer: Efficiency equals the biomass in the higher trophic level divided by the biomass in the lower trophic level, multiplied by 100.

questions.stem: State the link between energy loss and biomass loss between trophic levels.
questions.modelAnswer: Energy is stored within biomass, so any loss of energy between trophic levels appears as a loss of biomass too.

questions.stem: Explain why the efficiency figure is always below 100 percent.
questions.modelAnswer: The efficiency figure stays below 100 percent because losses from uneaten parts, egestion, heat and excretion always remove some energy or biomass before the next level.

questions.stem: A farmer wants more beef from the same pasture. Explain the limit.
questions.modelAnswer: Only about 10 percent of the grass biomass becomes cattle biomass, so the pasture cannot yield unlimited beef however well it is managed.
